newsitem.title: USA: Drug traffickers now are main Latam threat - US.
newsitem.headline: Drug traffickers now are main Latam threat - US.

text.p: Drug trafficking and international crime posed the main threats to security and democracy in Latin America in the post-Cold War years, senior U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

Addressing U.S. and Latin American military officers and defence officials at a conference on Western Hemisphere Strategy, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson praised Latin American armed forces for supporting civilian governments and hailed the growing respect for human rights among militaries with a long history of repression.

But as the threat from left-wing revolutionaries receded and with Cuba unable to wield military and political influence as before, new challenges had arisen and the region's nations must co-operate to tackle them, they said.
"Narcotics trafficking, international crime, migrant smuggling, terrorism and environmental degradation ... these are our enemies," Richardson said.

"The illegal drug trade and related activities such as money laundering and increasing violence and terrorism undermine fragile democratic institutions, distort economies and hinder long-term growth. We are dedicated to working cooperatively with nations in the hemisphere in the fight against narcotics."
Cohen echoed Richardson's words, saying the military threat from communist Cuba, once seen by Washington as a major source of destablization in Latin America, had diminished.
"Cuba stand as an anamoly more than anything else today," he told a news conference. "I think that its power is waning, if it still exists at all, in terms of threatening its neighbours."

But academics at the symposium, organised by the United States Southern Command, said Latin American armies might not necessarily share Washington's priorities. Some armies were reluctant to get involved in the drug war because they viewed it as police work while their main task was internal security and defending national frontiers.
"A lot of them feel they are doing it at the behest of the United States. They don't relish it," Ambler Moss, director of the University of Miami's North-South Centre, told Reuters.
It also exposed armed forces to corruption as drug traffickers tried to bribe officers, he said.

Boosting the armed forces' role in fighting drug trafficking could also weaken the development of civilian rule, George Vickers of the Washington Office on Latin America said. "It's quite worrisome. It seems to send a contradictory message. As they search for a new role it gives them a reason for aquiring new weapons and keeping strong forces."
